name: Whisky and cigar voice fad

lead: Some online circles associate cigars, smoking and whisky with a deep, husky voice that sounds attractive. No source reviewed documents the fad's origin.

Medical references do describe a real link between smoking and a lower, hoarse voice: smoke exposure causes fluid buildup in the vocal folds (Reinke's edema), which slows vibration, lowers pitch and causes hoarseness. The attractiveness claim rests on anecdote.

paras: Followers of the idea smoke or drink with the aim of getting a huskier voice over time.
Documented harms include laryngeal cancer risk, precancerous changes, breathing difficulty from swelling and, in some cases, surgery. The voice change reflects vocal fold disease.

chain: Smoking and drinking irritate vocal cords
angle.text: The aim is a deep, husky voice from smoke and alcohol irritating the vocal cords. The lowered voice is documented in some smokers as a result of vocal fold swelling; its attractiveness rests on anecdote.

lead: The whisky and cigar voice fad refers to the idea, discussed in some online circles, that smoking and drinking produces a deep, husky voice that is attractive. The sources reviewed contain no material on its history or on community discussions of it.

Medical references do describe a real link between smoking and a lower, hoarse voice: smoking is the leading cause of Reinke's edema, which slows vocal fold vibration, lowers pitch and causes hoarseness.[1] The same entry reports that smoking increases the risk of precancerous changes, and smoking is associated with laryngeal cancer.[1][2]

paras: In Reinke's edema the vocal folds become floppy and gelatinous, with added mass that lowers pitch.[1][2] Alcohol is listed among substances to limit in vocal hygiene guidance, along with tobacco and caffeine. Reflux, which alcohol is among the factors linked to, is also associated with hoarseness.[3]
Clinicians describe the voice change as a symptom of disease; surgery may be needed in severe cases, and breathing difficulty can occur.[1]
No studies found on this practice as a voice-enhancement approach. Related clinical literature on smoking and Reinke's edema describes it as a disease process.
